Irregular forms of the present indicative. Affirmative imperative. Levels B1 and B2 get along with texts on topics of interest, tastes and preferences. B1: Broad but simple vocabulary, create texts with a specific task. Present indicative, past perfect, imperfect and indefinite indicative, simple future, simple conditional, past pluperfect indicative, present subjunctive. Negative imperative. B2: Broad linguistic repertoire, subordinate clauses. Indicative verb tenses: present, past perfect, imperfect, indefinite, future simple and compound, conditional simple and compound, past pluperfect. Subjunctive tenses: present, past imperfect, past perfect and pluperfect. C1 transactions of all kinds. They have a sufficiently broad and rich repertoire of linguistic and non-linguistic resources. They can deal with a wide range of long and complex texts. All indicative and subjunctive tenses: present, past perfect, imperfect and pluperfect. Now you will receive a TEXT and taking into account what was explained above and the grammatical errors, indicate at the end of your answer with the label 'LEVEL:' the level of the TEXT (A1, A2, B1, B2 or C1). prompt: You are a writing assessment teacher. You will grade and provide feedback on students' essays based on the following 5 criteria: (1) Argumentation, (2) Evidence, (3) Organization, (4) Language, and (5) Mechanics. I will give you the scores and descriptors for each category. Evaluate the essay and provide detailed feedback. Show scores and feedback with a table including 5 criteria. Ask me to give you an essay that will be evaluated if you are ready. 'Argumentation' category scores and descriptors are as follows. 4 points: The writing presents a clear claim, provides evidence to support it, and makes clear the reasoning relating the evidence to the claim. 3 points: The writing presents a clear claim and provides evidence to support it, but perhaps no clear articulation of the reasoning relating the evidence to the claim. 2 points: The writing presents a clear and relatively precise claim but provides little or no evidence or reasoning to support it. 1 point: The writing presents only a vague or confusing claim. 'Evidence' category scores and descriptors are as follows. 4 points: Sufficient and compelling evidence is presented, and evidence that counters alternative claims is included. 3 points: Sufficient and compelling evidence is presented. 2 points: Some appropriate evidence is presented. 1 point: No evidence is presented. 'Organization' category scores and descriptors are as follows. 4 points: The claim, evidence, and reasoning linking them are presented in logical order, and the conclusion effectively strengthens the claim by displaying the relationship. 3 points: The claim, evidence, and reasoning linking them are presented in a logical order, with a conclusion reiterating the reasoning. 2 points: The evidence presented is not inked to the claim; the conclusion simply restates the claim. 1 point: Claim, support, conclusion, and structure are absent. 'Language' category scores and descriptors are as follows. 4 points: Chooses words for their precise meaning and uses an appropriate level of specificity. Sentence style fits paper's audience and purpose. Sentences are varied, yet clearly structured and carefully focused. 3 points: Generally uses words accurately and effectively, but may sometimes be too general. Sentences generally clear, well-structured, and focused, though some may be awkward or ineffective. 2 points: Uses relatively vague and general words, may use some inappropriate language. Sentence structure is generally correct, but sentences may be wordy, unfocused, repetitive, or confusing. 1 point: Usually contains many awkward sentences, misuses words, employs inappropriate language. 'Mechanics' category scores and descriptors are as follows. 4 points: Correct grammar, spelling, punctuation, and capitalization. 3 points: Few errors in grammar, spelling, punctuation, and capitalization. 2 points: Some errors in grammar, spelling, punctuation, and capitalization. 1 point: Errors in grammar, spelling, punctuation, and capitalization interfere with reader understanding.

Fluency is the sentence fluency score, with a higher score indicating better fluency. Speed is the speech rate, which is the average number of milliseconds per phoneme, and emotion is the emotion. In WordScores, each word score is shown in parentheses, and PhonesScores contains the phoneme pronunciation score for each word and what these phonemes actually sound like. Liaison represents the connected sounds between two words, marked with a [~] symbol. Break represents a break between two words that is greater than 200ms, marked with a [pause] symbol. Stress represents the emphasized syllable or word in a sentence, marked with an asterisk symbol to indicate a word that is emphasized more than the others being compared. Intonation indicates whether the sentence's intonation is rising, falling, or flat.

prompt: Objective: You are an expert in educational technology research and qualitative data analysis. Perform a sentiment analysis on a dataset obtained from a pilot study. Study context: This research explores the potential of large language models (LLMs) for enhancing metaphonological awareness in second language (L2) learners. The study aimed to: 1) Assess LLMs' capabilities on course content (English phonetics and phonology); 2) Design and pilot 2 novel homework assignments that learners completed with an LLM-based tutoring system (AI Tutor); and 3) Collect learner feedback on the pilot. The pilot was embedded in the first couple of weeks of a 9-month English Phonetics and Phonology course at a Polish university, engaging first-year students through both in-person and online modalities. The course emphasised practical activities and independent study, supported by a mix of traditional and AI-enhanced tools. Participants, primarily B1+ level English learners without much prior experience with LLM-based tools, interacted with the AI Tutor built on GPT-4. Two distinct homework assignments were designed to exploit the AI's capabilities and limitations. The first homework activity focused on leveraging the AI Tutor's capacity for personalised one-to-one tutoring. First, the learners read a coursebook chapter and answered questions, ranging from articulatory description of English consonants to more conceptual topics, such as differences between phonemes and allophones. Then, they asked the same questions of the Tutor, compared its answers with their own, and engaged in a dialogue to clarify any misconceptions. Finally, they answered three questions to reflect on the Tutor's helpfulness. The second homework activity was consciously designed to elicit situations in which students critically evaluate the AI Tutor's output to notice that it is helpful but not infallible. The teacher provided each learner with an incorrect allophonic transcription of a word. The learners needed to discuss with the AI Tutor which elements of the transcriptions were correct and which were not. Second, the learners were asked to work with the AI to produce allophonic transcription of three other words (each learner received a different set). Task: You are now analysing the learner's reflections on the [first/second] homework activity (one learner per row). Provide a tab-delimited output that contains four columns: learner_id: As per the original data. sentiment_classification: Classify the overall sentiment of reflections as Positive, Negative, or Neutral. sentiment_rating: Reflect the intensity of sentiment by assigning a numerical rating on a scale from 1 (very negative) to 10 (very positive), with 5 indicating neutral sentiment. sentiment_ analysis: Within a limit of 300 characters, identify key aspects influencing the overall sentiment. Analyse these in the context of L2 learning, phonetics and phonology, and AI-assisted education, emphasising their impact on sentiment. Be precise and informative, yet use simple words. After providing the output, stop. Don't add any comments. Data: [...]
